quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hold your palm a few centimetres from your lips and say the word slowly. Does the first sound land a small puff of air on your hand?
quests.explanation: 'Pen' opens with /p/. Your lips seal, pressure builds, and the release sends a quick puff of breath out before the vowel, with no vibration in your throat. /b/ uses the same lip closure but is voiced, so it comes out softer with far less puff.
quests.mouthPosition: Seal both lips, let the air build for a beat, then pop them apart. Your throat stays quiet; the puff should reach your palm before 'en' begins.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Rest two fingertips on your throat and say only the first sound. Do you feel a buzz under your fingers while your lips are still shut?
quests.explanation: 'Boat' starts with /b/, the voiced partner of /p/. Your vocal cords are already vibrating while the lips are closed, so the release is soft and nearly puff-free. A hard burst on your hand means you've drifted toward /p/, and the word starts to sound like 'poat'.
quests.mouthPosition: Press your lips together and start humming in your throat before they open. Let them part gently into 'oat' rather than popping them.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Pinch your nose lightly and say the word. If the first sound gets stuck or changes, your breath was travelling somewhere other than your mouth.
quests.explanation: 'Milk' begins with /m/. The lips close exactly as they do for /b/, but the soft palate drops, so voiced air escapes through your nose instead of building up behind the lips. That's why /m/ can be stretched ('mmm-ilk') and /b/ cannot.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips, relax your jaw, and hum so the sound flows out through your nose. Open the lips only when you move into 'ilk'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hold a thin strip of paper just below your lips as you say the word. Does it flutter from a quick rush of air right after the first sound?
quests.explanation: 'Tea' begins with /t/. The tongue tip taps the bumpy ridge just behind your upper front teeth and springs away with a burst of breath. Nothing is buzzing in your throat while the tongue is up; with /d/ the voice would already be running and the burst would be softer.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your top teeth, hold for a beat, then flick it down with a small burst of air.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hum a low note and begin the word without breaking it. Does the hum survive the first sound?
quests.explanation: 'Dog' opens with /d/. The tongue touches the same ridge as /t/, but the voice switches on during the contact, so the release is soft and buzzy rather than crisp and airy. Fingers on your throat will feel the vibration start before the vowel arrives.
quests.mouthPosition: Put your tongue tip on the ridge behind the upper teeth and start your voice while it's still there. Release smoothly into 'og' with no extra puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hold a small mirror or a cold spoon under your nostrils and start the word. Does the surface fog up during the first sound?
quests.explanation: 'Nose' starts with /n/. Your tongue sits in exactly the position it takes for /d/, but the soft palate is lowered so voiced air flows out through your nose instead of being trapped and released. That's why the mirror clouds and why /n/ can be held as a steady hum.
quests.mouthPosition: Rest your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth and hum, letting the sound run out through your nose. Drop the tongue away as you glide into 'ose'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Focus on the very back of your mouth. When the first sound lets go, does air rush out first, or does voice come first?
quests.explanation: 'Cool' begins with /k/: the back of the tongue presses the soft palate and releases with a puff of air and no voice. The spelling with C is just another way of writing the same sound as K. /g/ shares the tongue position but adds a buzz and loses the puff.
quests.mouthPosition: Raise the back of your tongue until it presses the soft part of the roof of your mouth, then let go with a quick puff. Your tongue tip rests down behind your lower teeth.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Find the spot where the back of your tongue rests when you say the 'ng' in 'sing'. Start the word from there. Is your voice already humming when the tongue lets go?
quests.explanation: 'Go' starts with /g/, the voiced twin of /k/. The back of the tongue closes against the soft palate while your voice is already running, so the release is smooth and unpuffed. A crisp burst would push the word toward 'co'.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the back of your tongue against the soft palate and start the voice before you release. Let it drop smoothly into the 'oh'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Watch what your tongue tip does. Does it tap the ridge behind your teeth, or stay low while the back of the tongue does the work?
quests.explanation: 'Cup' starts with /k/, made at the back of the mouth. The tip of the tongue stays down while the back lifts to the soft palate. Moving the action to the front, at the ridge behind the teeth, gives you 'tup'. Here it's place, not voicing, that separates the two sounds.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the tip of your tongue resting behind your lower teeth. Raise only the back to touch the soft palate, then release with a puff into 'up'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Try holding the first sound of this word for a full breath before adding the vowel. Can you keep it going, or does it stop dead?
quests.explanation: 'Sun' starts with /s/, a fricative: the tongue tip comes close to the ridge without sealing, so a narrow stream of air keeps hissing through. /t/ closes completely and can only release once, which is why it can't be stretched. 'Sssun' works; 'tttun' doesn't.
quests.mouthPosition: Bring your tongue tip close to the ridge behind your top teeth without touching it, and push a thin stream of air over it. Teeth close together, lips relaxed.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Watch your mouth in a mirror as you begin the word. Do your lips press together, or does your bottom lip tuck up toward your top teeth?
quests.explanation: 'Fan' begins with /f/. The bottom lip rests lightly against the upper teeth while air is pushed through the narrow gap, making a steady, quiet hiss. /p/ shuts both lips completely and releases in one burst. Lip-to-lip is a stop; lip-to-teeth is a hiss you can keep going.
quests.mouthPosition: Rest your upper teeth lightly on your bottom lip and blow air through the gap without using your voice. Don't close the lips.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Feel the air just after your tongue touches the ridge. Is it sealed in and released once, or does it keep leaking out?
quests.explanation: 'Toy' opens with /t/: the tongue tip seals against the ridge, air builds up, and a single burst follows. Because the seal is complete there's no ongoing hiss. If you hear steady air before the vowel, it's slipped into /s/ and 'toy' sounds like 'soy'.
quests.mouthPosition: Seal the tongue tip firmly on the ridge behind your top teeth, then pull it away in one quick movement so the air pops out.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Pay attention to the vowel just before the last sound. Is it short and clipped, or long and drawn out?
quests.explanation: 'Cap' ends in /p/. English shortens the vowel before a voiceless final consonant, so the 'a' is brief and the word stops crisply as the lips close. With /b/ ('cab') the vowel stretches and the voice keeps buzzing into the closure. Vowel length is one of the clearest clues.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish by pressing your lips together to stop the air, with your throat quiet. You can release a tiny puff or simply hold the closure.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Stretch the vowel a little longer than feels natural. Does your voice keep running all the way into the final tongue tap?
quests.explanation: 'Bed' ends in /d/. The voice carries through the vowel and into the tongue's closure on the ridge, and the vowel is noticeably longer than in 'bet'. Drop the voice too early and you've said a different word. Keep the buzz until the very end.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish by touching your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth while your voice is still running. Let the sound fade instead of adding a hard puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Feel your throat as the word ends. Is the buzz still there when the back of your tongue touches the roof, or has it already stopped?
quests.explanation: 'Bag' ends in /g/. The back of the tongue closes on the soft palate while the voice is still on, and the vowel is a little longer than it would be before /k/. A voiceless ending gives you 'back', an entirely different word.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the back of your tongue to the soft palate to close off the word, keeping your vocal cords vibrating until the closure. No strong puff afterwards.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Check your lips in a mirror on the first sound. If they meet, the action is at the front. If they stay apart, it's happening further back.
quests.explanation: 'Pool' starts with /p/, a front-of-the-mouth sound made with both lips. /k/ is made far back, where the tongue meets the soft palate, so the lips stay open and rounded for the next vowel. Watching the lips is the fastest way to separate the two.
quests.mouthPosition: Press both lips together, build up a little air, and release with a puff. The tongue can stay relaxed and low; the lips do all the work.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Find out which part of your tongue moves, the very tip or the back. Say the first sound very slowly and feel where it touches the roof of your mouth.
quests.explanation: 'Tall' begins with /t/, made by the tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper teeth. /k/ is made by the back of the tongue much further back, so 'call' and 'tall' feel different even though both are voiceless. Tip versus back is the whole contrast.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift only the tongue tip to the ridge behind your top teeth and flick it away with a light puff. The back of the tongue stays low.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: At the end of the word, notice which part of your mouth closes. Can you feel it deep near your throat rather than up front?
quests.explanation: 'Rock' ends in /k/. The back of the tongue rises to the soft palate and shuts off the air with no voice. Closing with the tongue tip instead would give you 'rot'. For a clear finish you can release a small puff or just hold the closure.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish by lifting the back of your tongue against the soft palate to stop the air. Tongue tip stays down, throat quiet.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hum a low note and start the word without breaking it. Where in the word, if anywhere, does the hum break?
quests.explanation: 'Girl' starts with /g/. The back of the tongue touches the soft palate while the vocal cords vibrate throughout, giving a soft voiced start. A sharp puff would turn it into 'curl'. Here the letter G stands for the hard sound, the same one you heard in 'go'.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the back of your tongue to the soft palate and voice through the closure, then slide into the 'er' vowel. No puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Notice the end of the word without opening your lips again. Is your throat still humming as they close?
quests.explanation: 'Web' ends in /b/. Both lips close and the voice continues through the closure, so the last moment of the word is soft and buzzy. Ending with /p/ would give 'wep' and shorten the vowel too. The lips do the same job for both; only voice and vowel length differ.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips at the end while your voice is still running and let the sound fade. Skip any strong puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say the word slowly and sleepily. Does the first sound feel soft and voiced, or crisp and airy?
quests.explanation: 'Day' begins with /d/. The tongue tip meets the ridge behind your upper teeth with the voice already on, so the sound is soft and slightly buzzy and your palm would feel almost no puff. A crisp puff would make it 'tay'.
quests.mouthPosition: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth, voice on, and release smoothly into the 'ay' vowel. Don't add extra air.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Your nose hums for both sounds you're choosing between. What differs is the closure: made by the lips, or by the tongue tip? Feel for it as you begin.
quests.explanation: 'Mouse' starts with /m/. It's a nasal, so voiced air flows through the nose while your lips are closed. /n/ is also nasal, but its closure is made by the tongue tip on the ridge with the lips open. Which articulator closes is what separates 'mouse' from 'nouse'.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips, hum through your nose, then open your lips into 'ouse'. The tongue can rest low and flat.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Ignore the G in the spelling and slow the word down. As it finishes, do your lips close, or does your tongue tip rise to the ridge?
quests.explanation: 'Sign' ends in /n/; the G is silent. The tongue tip rises to the ridge behind your top teeth and voiced air flows through the nose while your lips stay apart. If your lips closed at the end you'd be saying 'sighm'. Your ears, not the spelling, tell you the ending.
quests.mouthPosition: End with your tongue tip resting on the ridge behind your top teeth and hum through your nose. Keep your lips slightly apart.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The last letter is B, but does your mouth actually pop open there? Say the word and notice whether your lips finish with a hum through the nose or a burst.
quests.explanation: 'Lamb' ends in /m/; the B is silent. Your lips close and voiced air flows through the nose, so the word ends in a hum rather than a burst. Silent letters are a good reminder to trust what you hear and feel instead of what you see written.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips at the end and let the voice flow out through your nose. Don't release into a pop.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Two fingers on your throat, palm in front of your mouth. Which is stronger in the first sound: the throat buzz or the puff on your palm?
quests.explanation: 'Ten' begins with /t/, a voiceless tongue-tip stop: the throat stays quiet and a small puff follows the release. That puff helps keep 'ten' from sliding into 'den'. A clean /t/ needs a firm tongue contact and a clear release.
quests.mouthPosition: Press your tongue tip firmly against the ridge behind your upper teeth, then release with a small puff of air. Keep your throat silent.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: At the end of the word, can you keep the last sound going as long as you like? Or does it end the moment your lips or teeth touch?
quests.explanation: 'Roof' ends in /f/. Your upper teeth touch the bottom lip and air keeps hissing through the gap, so you can stretch the ending as long as your breath lasts. /p/ would shut the lips and end in a single pop, giving you 'roop'.
quests.mouthPosition: Rest your top teeth lightly on your bottom lip and let a steady stream of air flow out. Keep your voice off.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Imagine a candle a hand's length away. Could the first sound of this word make the flame flicker?
quests.explanation: 'Pie' starts with /p/. With no voicing to soften it, the burst of air after your lips open is strong enough to flicker a candle flame. With /b/ the voice takes over and the release is gentle, so the word would sound like 'buy'.
quests.mouthPosition: Press your lips together, hold the air for a beat, then release it with a clear puff. Your throat stays quiet until the vowel.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Compare the length of the vowel with the vowel in 'cap'. Which one does the word you heard sound closer to?
quests.explanation: 'Cab' ends in /b/. The vowel stretches and the voice carries into the closed lips, so the ending sounds soft and full. A voiceless /p/ would clip the vowel and make the word 'cap', a different word. Vowel length is the biggest clue for listeners.
quests.mouthPosition: Let the vowel run longer, close your lips with the voice still on, and release only gently. No extra puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say the first sound with your lips slightly open the whole time. Does the sound come out the same way?
quests.explanation: 'Nut' starts with /n/. The tongue tip rests on the ridge and voiced air passes through the nose, while the lips stay apart the entire time. /m/ needs them closed. That single difference separates 'nut' from 'mutt' at the very start.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the tongue tip to the ridge behind your top teeth, hum through your nose, then drop the tongue into 'ut'. Lips relaxed and slightly open.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Look at how close your tongue tip gets to the ridge. Does it touch and seal, or hover near enough to make a hiss?
quests.explanation: 'Sea' starts with /s/, a hiss made when the tongue tip hovers close to the ridge and air is squeezed through. /t/ would seal the tongue and pop, giving you 'tea'. Those two words share the same vowel, so the start alone carries the entire difference.
quests.mouthPosition: Bring the tongue tip close behind your upper teeth without touching, and push a thin, steady stream of air over it. Spread your lips slightly for the vowel.
